cards.title: Diagnose Whether You Are Overspending or Underspending on Google Ads
cards.summary: Google sits bottom-of-funnel and captures demand other channels create, so most accounts either over-invest or wrongly starve Google of budget.
cards.use_when: Setting annual or quarterly budget allocation across Google, Meta, TikTok and affiliates, or deciding whether to increase Google spend when the platform reports high ROAS.
steps: Recognise the two failure modes: (1) overspend — Google looks efficient because it captures bottom-intent demand generated by Meta, TikTok and affiliates, so you push budget into spend that isn't incremental; (2) underspend — you believe Google is only bottom-funnel so you cap it at e.g. $10k/month while spending millions on Meta, even though your category has large cold search volume your product could serve.
To test which camp you're in, look at whether backend revenue moves when you increase Google spend, not just the in-platform ROAS figure.
If backend revenue does not track budget increases, you are likely overspending and should hold or redistribute, not scale further.
If backend revenue is constrained only because you never funded Google beyond a token amount, investigate cold search demand for your category terms before dismissing the platform.
Treat the source's >$10k/month anecdote as an illustration of the pattern, not a threshold for your store.
caveats: The two-camp framing is the source's heuristic; real accounts sit on a spectrum.
Attribution overlap between Google and upper-funnel channels makes either error easy to misdiagnose from platform numbers alone.

cards.title: Consolidate Campaigns Before Segmenting Them
cards.summary: Campaigns learn in isolation, so splitting identical products across campaigns starves low-volume ones of conversion data and lowers ROAS.
cards.use_when: Auditing or restructuring campaign architecture (shopping, PMax, search) or when you see ROAS fall as you go down the campaign list.
steps: Map each campaign's 30-day conversion volume. If you run three shopping campaigns with 50, 20 and 10 conversions respectively, ignore the small amount of cross-campaign platform data sharing and model them as fully siloed.

The campaign with 10 conversions is modelling bids off 10 users' psychographic data — it cannot bid accurately and will underperform. This is why account structures typically show ROAS declining in line with conversion volume.
Merge products and budget into the highest-volume campaign to pool conversions (e.g. 90/month) so smart bidding has a larger dataset and produces more accurate auction bids.
Only re-segment once you can justify the split commercially — the default should be one campaign; each additional campaign must earn its place.
Validate any restructuring with backend revenue, since consolidated campaigns may look better in-platform for reasons unrelated to true incrementality.
caveats: Consolidation assumes products share margin profile, market and creative logic; merging different-margin or different-country products distorts bidding.
Platform-level data sharing exists to a degree; the silo model is a simplification for planning.

cards.title: The Four Justifications for Segmenting a Google Ads Account
cards.summary: Only brand vs non-brand, geography, margin/efficiency targets and product category justify splitting campaigns beyond the consolidated default.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to create an additional campaign for a product line, market or margin tier.
steps: Start from the default of one campaign; require heavy justification for every extra campaign.
1) Brand vs non-brand: never let a single PMax or shopping campaign cover both, because you want branded placements and cold acquisition managed separately.
2) Geography: selling in multiple countries always warrants campaign-level separation.

3) Margin or efficiency goals: a 70% gross-margin collection must not share a bidding strategy with a 35% margin collection. At a 300% target ROAS the 35% line is barely profitable while the 70% line is very profitable, and because Google usually can't see margin it will push all spend to whichever drives more revenue.
4) Product category: products that attract different personas (e.g. office chairs vs plants) should learn separately so each models its own audience.
When proposing a split, name which of the four variables it addresses — if none apply, consolidate.
caveats: The 70%/35% margin and 300% ROAS figures are illustrative.
Margin-based segmentation depends on having margin data available to feed the platform; otherwise you're relying on separate campaigns and bids.

cards.title: Convert SKAGs into Single-Topic Ad Groups
cards.summary: Responsive Search Ads need large impression pools to exit learning, so one-keyword ad groups should be replaced by themed groups of 10–20 keywords.
cards.use_when: Restructuring search campaign ad groups, or inheriting an account still running Single Keyword Ad Groups.
steps: Understand why SKAGs died: an RSA contains up to 15 headlines, 4 descriptions and other assets, producing roughly 2,700 combinations. Google split-tests these against each other, and testing realistically needs about a quarter-million impressions to resolve.
A single exact-match keyword will never deliver that volume, so the ad stays stuck in learning and cannot optimise.
Restructure into single-topic ad groups: e.g. 'general plumbing', 'emergency plumbing', 'affordable plumbing'. Under each theme, place 10–20 themed keywords rather than one.
Write ads tuned to the theme so they are contextually relevant to every keyword in the group; the dynamic RSA then adjusts which headlines serve based on which keyword in the theme triggered.

When auditing an existing SKAG account, transition to single-topic groups and compare performance — the source reports better results consistently across audited accounts, while acknowledging rare accounts where SKAGs still work.
caveats: The quarter-million-impression figure is the source's testing heuristic, not a platform-published threshold.
The source's demonstrated example is a service business; the same logic is applied by the source to ecommerce search campaigns.

cards.title: Fix the Seven Most Common Google Ads Setup Mistakes
cards.summary: A rapid audit list of configuration errors that quietly drain budget or corrupt measurement in ecommerce accounts.
cards.use_when: Running an account audit or onboarding a store's existing Google Ads account.
steps: 1) Don't use GA4 events as the primary conversion: the source reports a 10–15% (sometimes higher) attribution gap versus direct snippet code on the site.
2) Don't run a single asset group in a PMax campaign — build segmentation at asset-group level.
3) Don't pair broad match with Maximize Clicks: broad match needs a smart bidding strategy to work well.
4) Turn off display in search campaigns; the source rates display as one of the worst networks, especially for cold traffic.
5) Add negative keywords — both branded negatives on cold campaigns and general negatives in search campaigns.
6) Turn off auto-applied recommendations so Google stops making changes you didn't approve.
7) Set a naming convention: agency tag, region, campaign type (PMax/shopping/search), audience (cold/brand/theta), and optionally goal, so anyone can read the account.
caveats: The 10–15% GA4 gap is the source's observed figure and should be verified in your own setup.
Naming convention fields are the presenter's preference; adapt to your team.

cards.title: Set Up PMax Asset Groups with Matching Listing Groups
cards.summary: PMax's single biggest error is one default asset group or multiple asset groups that all share the same products.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce store.
steps: Know the mechanics: an asset group holds images, headlines and descriptions used for search, display, YouTube, Discover and Gmail placements; its listing group holds the products from the Merchant Center feed that serve on Shopping.
If you accept the default single asset group, everything is bundled and creative can't be matched to intent.
If you build multiple asset groups but forget to customise each listing group, every asset group still contains all products — the segmentation does nothing.

Four reasons to segment: (1) creative relevance — a shopper who viewed jeans should be retargeted with jeans imagery and copy, not random catalogue items; (2) audience signals work better when granular, since you can signal 'in market for jeans' instead of vague 'fashion'; (3) search themes become specific; (4) you gain visibility into performance by asset group, e.g. seeing that tops are outperforming jeans due to seasonality and reallocating budget.

Apply the rules of thumb: one asset group per product type (chairs/tables/lighting/decor, or hand tools/power tools/fasteners/accessories), at least 15 products per asset group, never one product alone (it will get little spend).
caveats: The 15-product minimum is a flexible heuristic that depends on SKU count.
The source advises a minimum of three and maximum of about 20 asset groups; beyond 20 most businesses lack the complexity to justify it.

cards.title: Use Brand Exclusions and Weigh What Actually Matters in PMax
cards.summary: Without brand exclusions a PMax campaign is effectively a retargeting campaign; the source ranks the variables that move PMax performance.
cards.use_when: Configuring or prioritising fixes inside an ecommerce PMax campaign.
steps: Exclude your brand from PMax. Two methods exist: (1) campaign settings → brand exclusions → add new brand, let Google index your branded terms and apply the brand list; (2) the newer capability to add negative keywords directly to PMax. The source recommends doing both as fail-safes so a missed variation is still caught by the list and vice versa.

After running PMax across ~250 accounts and consulting on ~400 more, the source ranks variables in this order: (1) the GMC feed — titles, descriptions, imagery (assuming PMax is prioritising Shopping); (2) brand exclusions; (3) asset and listing group structure plus the assets themselves; (4) bidding strategy; (5) audience signals and search themes.
Search themes and audience signals are signals, not targeting — they do not guarantee bids on those terms. Prioritise keywords that historically converted in your account rather than inventing them.

For mature accounts spending tens of thousands per month, the source reports audience signals and search themes are roughly a 1% lever at best; they matter mainly on new business, new product, new category or new asset group launches, where there is no conversion history.
Once a campaign has ~30 days of conversion data, Google bypasses the audience signal — the source states you could remove it with no performance impact.
Verify current interface locations for brand exclusion and negative keyword settings before acting, as Google changes these.
caveats: The ranking and agency-tested figures are the source's own observations, not published benchmarks.
The claim that audience signals stop mattering is explicitly flagged as potentially controversial.

cards.title: Run a Feed-Only PMax to Force Shopping Placement
cards.summary: Deleting asset groups leaves only the listing group, forcing PMax onto Shopping and display retargeting only.
cards.use_when: Fixing a PMax campaign that is leaking spend into YouTube or Gmail, or when you want PMax restricted to Shopping.
steps: Understand the mechanics: delete the asset groups from the campaign so only the listing group remains. PMax can then place only on Shopping and on display, and on display it can only show product tiles from the feed since there are no headlines or descriptions. This is effectively what Smart Shopping used to be.

Before launching, switch off the two settings that destroy feed-only campaigns: URL expansion (which otherwise adds URLs, scrapes information and auto-builds asset groups) and automatically created assets.

Use it reactively or strategically: in one source example, a client spending a couple hundred thousand per month saw clicks spike and ROAS drop ~20%; PMax had drifted from ~2% to ~10% of spend on YouTube and ~10% on cold Gmail. Moving to feed-only prevented those placements and the account resumed scaling.

Be aware of the Gmail click issue: a click is counted when a user opens the fake email, not when they reach your site, producing cheap-looking clicks that never convert — and angry customers who believe they're being emailed after unsubscribing.
You can also run a mixed structure: some categories as feed-only PMax, others with full asset groups.
caveats: The source calls this a context-dependent, nuanced strategy rather than a default setup.
Verify current PMax settings UI before applying, as Google changes option names and locations.

cards.title: Use Max Conversion Value to Gather Data, Then Move to Target ROAS for Stability
cards.summary: Target ROAS does not raise average performance so much as flatten week-to-week volatility; Max Conversion Value makes bigger bets.
cards.use_when: Choosing or changing the bidding strategy on a PMax or shopping campaign.
steps: Launch on Maximize Conversion Value to accumulate conversion data, then roll into Target ROAS once data exists — this matches how the platform is designed to be used.

Expect the trade-off: Max Conversion Value produces large up-and-down swings as the algorithm makes bigger bets; Target ROAS smooths the distribution. The source notes total performance over the same period is roughly comparable — the difference is day-to-day reliability.
When setting the initial Target ROAS, look at trailing ROAS and set slightly below it (e.g. trailing 420–430% → set 400%).

Then watch for the trap: repeatedly nudging Target ROAS upward (400% → 425% → 450% → 500%) squeezes spend down until a new equilibrium. It looks like improved media buying, but the campaign is restricting who it bids on — the pool narrows toward warm audiences and existing customers rather than new ones.

If you need reliable daily revenue and don't need to chase incremental cold acquisition on that campaign, the higher target is a reasonable trade — but if you're already tight on volume, prefer a lower target and more spend.
caveats: Figures like 400–500% target ROAS are illustrative examples of the trap, not benchmarks.
The source frames the choice as reliability versus reach, not strictly better versus worse.

cards.title: Build a Feeder Strategy: Cold Shopping Plus Warm PMax
cards.summary: A low-target-ROAS cold campaign reaches cheap auctions nobody else bids on, feeding a high-target-ROAS warm campaign that converts.
cards.use_when: Scaling cold new-customer acquisition on Google when PMax alone has plateaued and you suspect warm-traffic over-attribution.
steps: Set up two campaigns: (1) a broad, low-Target-ROAS campaign (source example as low as 50%, i.e. 0.5 ROAS) that will bid across the entire pool of users searching relevant terms; (2) a high-Target-ROAS campaign (source example 600%) that only targets warm, in-market, likely-to-buy users, often previous site visitors.

The logic: most advertisers only bid on the high-intent half of the user pool (people who have visited many sites and used purchase-relevant terms). Google sees the other half as low intent — first-time searchers with no site history — and almost nobody competes for those auctions, so clicks are cheap.
The cold campaign drives traffic cheaply; the warm campaign captures and converts it on second or third click. The source reports this works well across many accounts.
Practically, run standard shopping as the cold campaign (it is better at reaching cold audiences) and PMax as the high-target-ROAS retargeting leg.

Why this is needed: the source reports that in private discussions, major agency owners agree PMax substantially over-attributes — 50%+ of PMax conversions are repeat or warm customers it didn't acquire — while standard shopping under-attributes because PMax takes credit for the final click. Verified against ~250 accounts running PMax plus ~400 consulted ecommerce accounts.
caveats: The 0.5 and 6.0 ROAS levels are source examples; set your own bands against your margin and data.
The 50%+ over-attribution figure is an industry observation reported by the source, not a measured benchmark you can rely on for your account.
Feeder strategies require enough spend to fund a deliberately unprofitable cold campaign without hurting overall economics.

cards.title: Recognise PMax's Ceiling and Reframe the Allocation Question
cards.summary: PMax is strong for smaller accounts but plateaus; the useful question is what percentage of spend goes to PMax versus standard shopping.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep scaling PMax or redistribute budget into standard shopping.
steps: If you are spending roughly $15–20k/month or less, PMax is useful to get the account moving and scaling.

As you scale PMax further, expect it to plateau. In the source's testing on large accounts scaled to $100k–$300k/month, doubling PMax budget while in-platform ROAS stayed at 5x did not move backend revenue.

Two common reactions both fail: raising budgets further, or raising the target ROAS. Both push more spend into warm and repeat traffic, so the in-platform ROAS may rise while the campaign becomes a 'glorified retargeting campaign'.
Accept that once PMax plateaus, further cold growth requires layering in standard shopping.

Measure the right thing: run a controlled ramp — scale one campaign type by 2x over 30 days and compare with another account ramping the other — and check backend revenue, not the in-platform ROAS. The source reports standard shopping consistently produced better incremental backend revenue despite its in-platform ROAS dropping (e.g. 5x → 4x → 3x) while PMax's stayed at 5x.

Reframe the planning question from 'should I run PMax?' to 'what percentage allocation should PMax versus standard shopping get?' — the source suggests roughly 20–40% to PMax for mid-to-upper-market ecommerce, with the majority in standard shopping.
caveats: The 20–40% allocation and $15–20k/month threshold are the source's heuristics, not universal rules.
The ramp test is illustrative and confounded by account differences; treat results as directional.
Lead-gen businesses should read 'shopping' as 'search'.

cards.title: Choose Between the Three Standard Shopping Structures
cards.summary: Top-seller split, feeder strategy and labelizer automation suit different catalogue sizes and business models.
cards.use_when: Choosing a standard shopping campaign structure for an ecommerce catalogue.
steps: Structure 1 — top sellers split: put all top sellers in one standard shopping campaign and everything else in a second. This forces Pareto (aim for ~80% of spend on the top 20% of products) while keeping a testing budget on the long tail to promote new winners. Suitable for a large SKU count in a non-fashion category; not suitable for fashion or a 5–10 product business.
Structure 2 — feeder strategy: run standard shopping as the cold traffic engine feeding a high-target-ROAS campaign (see separate card).

Structure 3 — labelizer/flo boost tiers: split products into over-index, index, near-index, under-index and no-index based on 30-day rolling performance, with bidding strategy and budget tuned per tier. You can label manually for small catalogues or run an automated labelizer script that re-tiers products in real time.
The source only recommends the labelizer for catalogues with thousands of SKUs — for most businesses it adds segmentation complexity without enough upside.
Apply the same four segmentation justifications as everywhere else (brand, geography, margin, category) if you split further.
caveats: The source explicitly warns against the top-seller split for fashion and small catalogues.
80% of spend on the top 20% of products is a stated aim for that one structure, not a general rule.

cards.title: Keep 80–90% of Ecommerce Google Spend in Shopping, Not Search
cards.summary: Shopping listings convey image, price, promos and comparison context pre-click, so they convert better than search ads in ecommerce.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split budget between shopping and search campaigns for an ecommerce store.
steps: For ecommerce and retail, target roughly 80–90% of Google spend in shopping rather than search — the source's core recommendation for the category.

Reason: search ads give the user a headline, a description nobody reads and a couple of extensions. Shopping shows the product image, price, title, active promos or reviews, brand name and extensions, with about five competitors beside you so the shopper pre-selects the most relevant listing before clicking.

For visual categories like fashion this matters most: search ads for 'red dress' attract clicks from people who then bounce because the style isn't theirs; shopping ads filter that mismatch pre-click.

Exception to reverse the split: ecommerce businesses with a B2B component. The source reports search outperforms shopping there — e.g. selling bulk eyelashes to technicians and small businesses — because a business buyer often won't click a shopping listing whose price doesn't match the mental model of a business purchase.
Only push into search after you've saturated shopping and need additional volume.
caveats: The 80–90% allocation is the source's recommendation for ecommerce, not a measured optimum for every store.
The B2B exception is the source's observation and depends on your buyer type.
